title: Cortés sails from Cuba
summary: Governor Diego Velázquez had picked Cortés to lead an expedition to the newly sighted mainland, then tried to cancel it. Cortés leaves anyway, with 11 ships, about 500 soldiers, 16 horses and a few cannon.
significance: Technically Cortés was a rebel from the start. Much of what he did next, and wrote to the king, was about making that rebellion legal.
questions: Why did Velázquez try to stop Cortés?

title: A shipwrecked Spaniard joins at Cozumel
summary: On the island of Cozumel, Cortés finds Gerónimo de Aguilar, shipwrecked eight years earlier and enslaved by the Maya. He now speaks Yucatec Maya. A fellow castaway, Gonzalo Guerrero, refuses to leave: he has a Maya wife and children.
significance: The first link in the chain of translation that made the whole conquest possible.

title: Battle of Centla; Malintzin joins
summary: The Chontal Maya of Potonchán fight the newcomers. A cavalry charge decides it; the Maya had never seen horses. Afterwards they give the Spaniards gifts and twenty young women, among them a Nahuatl speaker the Spaniards baptise Marina.
significance: Malintzin, or La Malinche, spoke Nahuatl and Maya; Aguilar spoke Maya and Spanish. Together they let Cortés talk to the Aztecs. She became his most important adviser and the mother of his son.
questions: Who was La Malinche, and how is she remembered?

title: Landing at San Juan de Ulúa
summary: Cortés lands on Good Friday. Moctezuma's envoys arrive with rich gifts, including discs of gold and silver as big as cartwheels, and ask the strangers to leave. The gifts have the opposite effect.
significance: Moctezuma's painters made pictures of the ships, horses and guns for him. Whether he thought Cortés was the god Quetzalcoatl returning is a story most historians now think was invented after the conquest.
questions: Did the Aztecs think Cortés was a god?

title: The Totonacs rebel against the Aztecs
summary: The Totonac ruler of Cempoala, an Aztec tributary, complains of heavy tribute. Encouraged by Cortés, the Totonacs seize Moctezuma's tax collectors. Cortés secretly lets two go free to win Moctezuma's trust. Nearby his men found a town, Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz.
significance: The first Indigenous allies of the Spanish, and the first sign of how brittle the empire's hold on its subjects was. The new town's council named Cortés its captain, answering to the king instead of to Velázquez.

title: Cortés scuttles his ships
place: Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz
summary: After sending one ship to Spain with treasure and his case for the king, Cortés has the rest run aground and stripped, so that no one can sail back to Cuba.
significance: The popular story says he burned them. He didn't; but the message was the same: there was no going back.

title: The march inland begins
summary: About 300 Spaniards, with Totonac warriors and porters, leave the coast and climb toward the high plateau.
significance: From here the expedition depended entirely on Indigenous guides, food and allies.
wiki: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire

title: Battles with Tlaxcala
summary: Tlaxcalan armies under the young commander Xicotencatl attack the Spaniards repeatedly over several days. The Spaniards survive, barely, thanks to steel, crossbows, cannon and horses fighting in tight formation.
significance: Tlaxcala's leaders decided these strangers were more useful as allies against the Aztecs than as enemies.

title: Alliance with Tlaxcala
summary: The Spaniards enter Tlaxcala as guests. Its ruling council, including the elder Xicotencatl and Maxixcatzin, commits to an alliance against the Aztecs, their enemies of generations.
significance: The single most important decision of the conquest. Tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan warriors fought alongside Cortés, and Tlaxcala kept special privileges under Spanish rule for centuries.
questions: Why did Tlaxcala side with Cortés?

title: The Cholula massacre
summary: In the great holy city of Cholula, an Aztec ally, Cortés claims to uncover a plot to ambush him. His men and the Tlaxcalans kill thousands of unarmed Cholulans gathered in the main temple courtyard.
significance: Whether the plot was real is still argued over. Either way, the massacre sent a message of terror ahead of the Spaniards.

title: Cortés meets Moctezuma
summary: Crossing the pass between the volcanoes, the Spaniards see the valley and its island city below. Bernal Díaz later wrote that some soldiers asked whether it was all a dream. On the causeway, Moctezuma himself comes out to greet Cortés and lodges the Spaniards in a palace.
significance: One of the great meetings in world history. Moctezuma's welcome may have been courtesy, caution or a trap; the sources disagree.
questions: Why did Moctezuma let the Spaniards in?

title: Moctezuma taken hostage
summary: Using the killing of some Spaniards on the coast as a pretext, Cortés seizes Moctezuma and keeps him under guard in the Spaniards' quarters, ruling through him.
significance: For months a handful of Spaniards ran a vast empire through a captive emperor, collecting gold as they went.

title: Massacre at the Great Temple
summary: While Cortés is away on the coast, Pedro de Alvarado and his men attack the unarmed nobles dancing at the festival of Toxcatl in the temple precinct, killing hundreds.
significance: The city rose up and besieged the Spaniards in their palace. The Florentine Codex describes the slaughter in harrowing detail.
wiki: Massacre in the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan

title: Cortés defeats Narváez
summary: Velázquez sends Pánfilo de Narváez with a larger army to arrest Cortés. In a night attack in the rain, Cortés captures Narváez and wins over his men with promises of gold.
significance: Cortés nearly doubled his Spanish force. But Narváez's expedition had also brought smallpox.

title: Moctezuma dies
summary: Back in the besieged palace, Cortés has Moctezuma appeal to his people from a rooftop. Spanish accounts say he was struck by stones from his own subjects and died days later. Nahua accounts say the Spaniards killed him.
significance: The Mexica had already chosen a new ruler, his brother Cuitláhuac. The Spaniards' hostage was worthless.

title: La Noche Triste
stat: Perhaps half or more of the Spaniards and thousands of allies lost; estimates vary widely
summary: Cortés tries to slip out of the city at night along the western causeway. The Mexica spot the column and attack from canoes on both sides. Men weighed down with gold drown in the gaps.
significance: The 'sad night' was the worst Spanish defeat in the Americas. The Mexica had driven the invaders out of their city.
questions: How many people died on the Noche Triste?

title: Battle of Otumba
summary: Retreating round the lake toward Tlaxcala, the exhausted survivors are cut off by a huge Mexica army on open ground. Cortés and a few horsemen charge the enemy commander and seize his standard, and the Mexica army breaks.
significance: Had Otumba been lost, the expedition would have ended there. Tlaxcala took the survivors in.

title: Smallpox in Tenochtitlan
summary: A smallpox epidemic sweeps the Valley of Mexico. People who had never met the disease die in huge numbers. Emperor Cuitláhuac dies of it in early December after only about 80 days on the throne.
significance: Disease may have killed more people than all the fighting, and it struck the Mexica just as they had a chance to recover.
questions: How much did disease decide the conquest?

title: Cortés makes Texcoco his base
summary: Cortés returns to the valley and occupies Texcoco, the second city of the Triple Alliance, where a rival claimant, Ixtlilxochitl, takes his side. Behind him, in Tlaxcala, the shipwright Martín López is building brigantines in pieces.
significance: The Triple Alliance was splitting. Over the next months town after town around the lake changed sides.

title: Cuauhtémoc becomes emperor
summary: Cuauhtémoc, a young cousin of Moctezuma, is made huey tlatoani, great speaker, and prepares the city for siege.
significance: He became the hero of Mexican resistance. A statue of him stands on Mexico City's Paseo de la Reforma.

title: Thirteen brigantines launched
summary: The brigantines, carried in pieces over the mountains from Tlaxcala by thousands of porters, are assembled and launched on the lake through a canal dug by allied workers.
significance: Whoever controlled the lake controlled the island city. The brigantines would decide the siege.

title: The siege begins: the aqueduct is cut
summary: Spanish divisions take up positions at the ends of the causeways and cut the aqueduct that brings fresh water from the springs of Chapultepec. With them are tens of thousands of Indigenous allies.
significance: The start of an 80-day siege that would destroy one of the great cities of the world.
questions: Who really won the siege, the Spanish or their allies?

title: Cortés nearly captured
summary: A big assault toward the Tlatelolco market is lured into a trap at a breach in the causeway. Cortés is dragged off and only rescued at the last moment. Dozens of Spaniards are captured and sacrificed at the temple, in full view of their comrades.
significance: Some allies drifted away, believing Mexica predictions of victory. Cortés switched to slow, systematic destruction of the city.

title: Tenochtitlan falls
stat: Estimates of the dead in the siege run from tens of thousands to well over 100,000
summary: With the city in ruins, its people starving and dying of disease, Cuauhtémoc tries to escape across the lake by canoe. A brigantine captures him. The fighting ends.
significance: The end of the Aztec Empire. A Nahua song from the aftermath mourns that 'broken spears lie in the roads'.

title: The Purépecha kingdom submits
summary: The Purépecha, the Aztecs' great western rivals who had never been conquered by them, submit to Spain without a major battle.
significance: A sign of how quickly the old political world of Mesoamerica was collapsing.

title: Cortés made governor of New Spain
summary: King Charles V confirms Cortés as governor of New Spain. On the ruins of Tenochtitlan, a Spanish city is being built; its cathedral will rise beside the buried Great Temple.
significance: Mexico City became the capital of Spain's empire in North America. Cuauhtémoc was tortured for gold and, in 1525, executed.
